review:
[h1] The Best Game of the Series. [/h1]

A title that managed to become the game I enjoyed and liked the most while playing in the series. Outside of the franchise, it is an accomplished masterpiece in general. What sets it apart from most RE games is that there is depth to this game. Compared to other RE titles, you can form a bond with the main character, side characters, and villains. Yes, characters like Leon and Chris are also very important, but I don't think a bond like the one established with Ethan Winters across a single game was ever achieved. Personally, even though I like Chris more, this game is an absolute masterpiece. Instead of mindless enemies found in other entries of the series, there are much better bosses. Most of them have personality and thoughts of their own.

[h2] Story and Characters [/h2]

We continue with Ethan Winters, whom we know from the previous game. In this game, Ethan's story turns into a much more personal and emotional journey. Following the events of RE7, Ethan is no longer just someone trying to survive; he is a father willing to risk everything for his family. This adds a very strong motivation to the narrative. If you remember in the previous game, he couldn't make sense of what was happening at first and focused on escaping, and later focused on saving Mia.

At the center of the game stands the mysterious Mother Miranda and the four lords under her control. By four lords, I mean basically Miranda's mock children. One of the things that makes the story intriguing is these pseudo-children; each of these characters has a distinct personality and motivation. While Lady Dimitrescu is arrogant and overly confident in her power, Karl Heisenberg turns into a remarkably striking antagonist with his intellect and rebellious attitude. On the other hand, Salvatore Moreau, who is bullied within the family, tries to prove that he is someone of importance. Lastly, Donna Beneviento and Angie remain a bit more childish compared to the others and stick to their own devices. The tension and simmering hatred among these characters whom Miranda considers her so-called "family" adds an unexpected depth to the plot. I say unexpected because while these lords act like kittens in front of Miranda, they hold nothing back when talking behind her back :d At least Heisenberg and Dimitrescu complain quite a bit about this situation.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails?id=3684935701
We also see Chris GOATfield, one of the iconic characters of the series, in this game, and he plays a very crucial role. With his mysterious entrance at the beginning of the story and the truths revealed in later chapters, the game succeeds in hooking us and piquing our curiosity.

[h2] Gameplay and Mechanics [/h2]

Village delivers horror and action in a very balanced way. Throughout the game, we experience both classic survival horror and action-oriented shootouts. Although action picks up heavily after a certain point, the tension created early on when we barely have decent gear, along with Angie's intense sections, balances the gameplay nicely. The parts where we navigate the basement of Angie's house without getting caught by the Baby were great. Additionally, we shouldn't forget that our weapons are taken away here; leaving us defenseless in a way, which ramps up the tension of the environment.

Weapon variety and the upgrade system are heavily improved compared to the previous game. It has very satisfying gameplay, and enemy variety is sufficient. The pressure and constant sense of threat created by werewolves and similar creatures in the village are executed very well. In some places, we can see them watching us from the rooftops, which I think is one of those details that enhances the gameplay. Lastly, because each boss fight offers a different gameplay dynamic, the game's pacing remains lively at all times.

[h2] Graphics and Atmosphere [/h2]

One of Village's strongest aspects is without a doubt its art design. The snow-covered village with its dark tone, gothic-architecture castles, gloomy mansions, and industrial areas are visually stunning. On 4K Ultra settings, the game looks extremely detailed and lifelike. Lighting, character models, and environmental designs are very well done. Just like other games in the franchise and their REMAKE versions, optimization is exceptional. I wasn't expecting it to offer such fluid gameplay with these visuals at 4K.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails?id=3684943433
The game is also very successful in terms of atmosphere. Ambient audio, howling wind, and the screeches of enemies keep the player on edge constantly. This further reinforces the dark and menacing vibe of the village.

[h2] Music and Sound Effects [/h2]

Sound design is one of the most critical elements completing Village's atmosphere. Ambient sounds, enemy effects, and gunfire are high quality. Especially the music and sound effects used during tense moments successfully elevate the pressure on us. We can see this clearly in one of my favorite sections, where we are chased by the Baby in Angie's house. The music utilized towards the finale amplifies the emotional impact of the scenes and supports the dramatic tone of the story. They delivered a magnificent finale...

[h2] Technical and Performance [/h2]

Technically, it offers rock-solid performance. Thanks to being well-optimized, it delivers a smooth experience even at high resolutions and graphical presets. Throughout my extensive playtime, I did not encounter severe performance issues or distracting technical bugs. It provides a stable experience.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails?id=3684965339
There is one more thing I want to mention here. I couldn't take screenshots in this game. Pressing F12 played the notification sound, but it wasn't saving any screenshots. I noticed this past the halfway mark of the game, and it really bummed me out. After realizing it, I took screenshots using AMD's software. When I researched the problem, I saw that a significant number of people experienced this issue; it is most likely a bug related to the game itself. While it doesn't affect gameplay, it is a bit frustrating for people like me who upload screenshots to Steam.

[h2] Overall [/h2]

In short, RE Village is a title that successfully strikes the balance between horror and action, possesses a powerful atmosphere, and is technically very solid. For me, it is simply a masterpiece. With its unforgettable characters, impressive art direction, and smooth gameplay, it became my favorite entry in the series. Combining horror elements rooted in the franchise's heritage with modern action, you should definitely give this title a try. Just don't forget to play RE7 beforehand :)

Make no mistake: the environment isn’t interactive, it’s mostly there to set a majestic mood while leaving just enough visual cues to push you forward. This game is far from clever, and the puzzles are about as hard as they were in the recent remakes. But they’re enough to make some players feel clever, and that’s all you can ask. And the backdrop for these simplistic puzzles almost never gets old to tour. Outside of the village and the castle, the story takes you to the expected tropes of past Resident Evil titles, but plays with your expectations enough to keep it engaging and surprising.

A mercantile system also returns in the very large body of the Duke, who lords over the proceedings with a watchful eye.
After buying one of the many upgrades for your weapons (which persist in future playthroughs), the Duke will cheerfully tell you to “have a wonderful adventure.”

The game is the narrative sequel to Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, picking up the story three years on. Ethan and Mia are parents now, trying to live out the wholesome family dream. It doesn’t take long for the action to kick in though as Chris Redfield interrupts the happy family and Ethan finds himself wandering into the terrifying hellscape of the village.

Whilst ‘village’ is the name of the game, you are not confined to this one location. It would be fair to say that the village is just the centre of this complicated and intricate world and the game does guide you in the general direction of the story, but you are also free to explore, and you are rewarded for this exploration.

- Open-world Resident Evil works well and is complemented by fun optional content
- Remarkable graphics and sound design create a new immersion benchmark for the series
- Face-twisting horror plot with some seriously sinister sequences

- The story looks the part but doesn’t explore its most interesting ideas

Resident Evil Village released exactly a year ago, but I wasn’t sure if my old PC would be able to run the game properly, so I decided to wait until I’d upgraded. Now that I’ve finally been able to play it, I can say that it does mostly live up to the hype. This is an excellent game which deserves all the positive reviews and awards.

[h1]The Good[/h1]

-	Feels like a survival horror game. Every enemy is dangerous, and your ammo and health recovery items are limited. Sometimes its better to just avoid enemies and save bullets.

-	Several different weapons that all feel good to use, including dagger, pistol, shotgun, sniper rifle, magnum, proximity mine and pipe bomb.

-	Good enemy variety including werewolves, vampires, flying demons, zombies, and unique boss monsters. Werewolves and zombies can wield weapons such as sword, axe, and bow.

-	Some enemies can be weakened by using environmental effects, or shooting them in a specific weak point.

-	Find hidden treasures which can be sold to a trader, allowing you to buy upgrades for your weapons.

-	Story is better than most Resident Evil games, although that’s not a high bar.

-	Voice acting is very good.

-	Controls are fully rebindable and work great on mouse and keyboard.

-	Took me 13 hours to finish.

-	I didn’t have any problems with bugs, crashes or framerate.

[h1]The Bad[/h1]

-	First two hours feel very scripted as you frequently get captured in cutscenes, escape, run down narrow tunnels/corridors, and repeat the cycle.

[h1]The Recommendation[/h1]

Anybody who hasn’t played Resident Evil Village yet should definitely do so when you get the chance. The story is a direct sequel to Resident Evil 7, so make sure you’ve played that game first.

As I've been expecting since the game's announcement, it was great. The story expands Resident Evil's lore and explains quite a lot of stuff. The gameplay as always is awesome, it's clunky but super satisfying. I like the concept of having to defeat 4 lords in order to face your main threat and i like the way it was implemented in the game. There are 4 areas and each area has it's own bosses and enemies.

First one is Castle Dimitrescu. I loved exploring the castle and i think they did a great job with the design and the atmosphere of the castle. Fighting the daughters Bela, Cassandra and Daniela and killing Alcina Dimitrescu herself at the end happened a little sooner and faster than i thought since they were hyped a lot but it makes sense since there are many more areas to go through in the game.

Second one is House Beneviento and i think i can say that this one is my favorite! It's like the Silent Hills game we never got to play and i freaking loved it. There are no common enemies in this house because it's more based off with puzzles and horror elements. I was shocked and terrorized by some of the things in the house but i won't spoil it because i think it's better if you go in there totally blind, it was an amazing experience playing through this part of the game.

Third one is Moreau's Reservoir. It was a disgusting place just like Moreau himself lol, I don't think it was the best but it was definitely interesting to go through, I liked the general atmosphere of it and Moreau turning into a giant fish like the one in Resident Evil 4 was fun to fight against.

Fourth and the last one is Heisenberg's Factory and even though I like this area I think it overstayed it's welcome. The concept of it is not the most interesting but also not the worse so i thought it'd be okay but since it's one of the longest parts of the game i remember thinking 'okay I've had enough let's leave this place now' but it has some interesting enemies and boss fights so it wasn't that bad.

Apart from all these areas there is the Village which is where the whole game is set in and i must say that i love it! The design of the village is amazing and i liked coming back to it as a hub area after every once in a while and there was always something to do before leaving again to go for a different location.

The game wasn't too hard, at least on the standard difficulty. My biggest complaint is that the puzzles were too easy, most of them didn't even require you to think carefully about what you're supposed to do. The game also has lots of replayability with the weapons, extra game modes and a new difficulty you can unlock by completing challenges which is great!

Overall, this game has great graphics, an amazing optimization (works in 60 fps on my GTX 1650), great bosses, some scary and intense moments and a decent story to tell. As a die hard fan of the Resident Evil series for a long time I strongly recommend you to experience this game, I don't think you'll regret it.

So, to put this into context, I hadn't played a Resident Evil game before, although I'd played the entire original Alone in the Dark trilogy, which was the inspiration for the originals. I also knew a bunch of things about most of the games at a surface level, but not much.

What made me decide to purchase this game is that I saw someone said it wasn't too scary. I saw this as a good thing. And yeah, it has the perfect blend of action vs. horror vs. what I'd like to call "old-school running around". By that I mean, exploring, solving light puzzles, etc.

And what I really liked about this whole blend is that it really felt like one of the older games transposed faithfully to modern sensibilities and tech. For one, I could imagine a RE1-style demake of this super easily. But most importantly, to use the Fallout franchise as an example... you know how Fallout 4 is arguably more a "Fallout-themed" game than an actual Fallout game? RE8 doesn't suffer from this problem at all, when you might have expected it to. It feels super faithful to the DNA of the series. And yeah, the caveat is that this is coming from someone who DIDN'T play any of the other games, but my point is that it felt enough like an older horror game made modern, in all the good ways.

The writing is good, the characters are good, the art direction is very solid, the technical presentation a liiiittle bit uneven (but good), the music is... forgettable, but that's fine, sometimes it's just not meant to be. No complaints about any of that.

My only complaint would be that I would've liked to have a "natural" way to tell when you have completely looted a room. Near the end of the game I was basically constantly opening & closing my map every time I picked something up to see if the room I was in had turned blue. Maybe a little chime or a line from Ethan would have been far better.

Overall, I have to say I would definitely recommend this game just on the basis of being a really great middle point between horror and action. And 90% of the horror is more "tension" than "psychological". There is only ONE straightforward horror segment in the entire game, and believe me, you'll know when you get to it... haha.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]

Resident Evil Village is a first-person shooter survival horror developed by Capcom. The game is set in the present time, three years following the events of RE 7. Once again, the player assumes the role of Ethan Winters, who, after an unfortunate series of events, finds himself separated from his family and stranded in a remote Romanian village. Here, he will set himself on a journey to save his family and, at the same time, survive the dreadful and unforgiving place.

By far, its story is my favorite in the entire series. The writers have surprisingly taken the Resident Evil narrative to a whole new level, and that’s something I didn’t think I’d ever say. Ethan’s arduous journey to rescue his family is convincing, immersive, and full of mysteries and twists, with memorable moments and characters — definitely an experience that will stick with me for a while.

[h3]A True Horror Experience[/h3] 

The game’s heavy, bleak, and terrifying atmosphere is remarkable. Wandering within the various bewildering and interconnected rooms of Castle Dimitrescu, exploring decrepit sheds, and running in the claustrophobic corridors of a colossal factory definitely felt like a dose of adrenaline. At all times, I couldn’t help but feel this eerie and disturbing feeling of vulnerability and anxiety — always expecting a jump scare or something of the sort at every turn and corner. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2483196646

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]

Gameplay-wise, this title is beyond excellent. From frantic combat to exciting exploration, everything is fluid, well-crafted, and entertaining. Once again, Capcom opted to deviate a little from their last iteration and give Village a more significant focus on the action. At first, I was slightly skeptical about it, as the last thing I wanted was this to be just another mediocre title, with some cheap Michael Bay-style sort of action segments and uninspired gameplay — yes, I’m talking to you, RE 6. Though, to my surprise and satisfaction, it wasn’t anything like that. In Village, they flawlessly attained the precise equilibrium between action and horror, essentially creating the perfect incorporation of RE 4 and 7 into one. Hence, even if you are not fond of this slightly more action-focused turn the game took, you shouldn’t be all worried; because, in the end, the game still manages to be a true survival horror, truthful to its roots.

The pleasant combat mechanic is one of the key features that made this title stand out the most. Whether gunning down a crowd of enemies who dare stand in your way, or just trying to protect yourself with a mere knife, Village’s combat plays fluidly and actually strives to keep the player engaged at all times. In order to stand your ground against the myriad of repulsive monstrosities, you can count on an immense and diversified arsenal that will help you send your foes to the other plane of existence. I’m really fond of the game’s large weapon assortment and how the guns work; each weapon in the game, from shotguns to hand cannons, is unique and feels totally authentic and pleasant to handle and shoot. And things don’t end there: during the journey, the player can additionally find a plethora of attachments to enhance their guns, these varying from extended magazines, barrels, foregrips, and even scopes.

While the game indeed recycles some of its predecessor’s core gameplay mechanics, it also brings plenty of additional features to the table, as well as tweaks to pre-existing ones. One of my favorites is that Ethan can now parry basic enemy attacks in addition to blocking them — which can be pretty useful; it certainly saved my life countless times. The crafting system was also further improved, and it is much simpler and quicker to craft your items this time. Instead of the old mechanic of “combining items” present in pretty much all previous iterations, here, crafting has its own exclusive tab where you can quickly assemble your items by pressing one mere button. And, surprisingly enough, Village has a pretty interesting hunting and cooking mechanic — which works in a very simplified manner. 

Scattered throughout the map, you can find a variety of animals to hunt, ranging from pigs to fishes and even goats. Once you kill any of the animals, it will drop a piece of meat, which can be delivered to the merchant to brew your selected desired meal. Eating certain dishes will highly improve Ethan’s overall stats permanently, such as health, movement velocity, and even how much damage he can take in fights. This cooking mechanic is indeed a very welcomed feature; even with its simplicity, it still is one of the best additions to the title. 

One aspect that the RE series is well known for and nearly constantly delivers in great fashion is, definitely, the boss fights — and here, it’s no different. Village has some of the most charismatic bosses and thrilling battles of the series. Every boss encounter plays uniquely, with each one of them having their own distinctive move sets, attack patterns, and weak spots the player must exploit to prevail in the fight. Even though I didn’t find them very arduous opponents (besides the final one), standing your ground against all the daunting monsters on the hardest difficulty certainly made me break a sweat.

To my surprise, the optional bosses are back in Village. There are five of them you can encounter as you progress in the narrative. Even though they aren’t as creative or their fights as unique as the main villains, I still had lots of fun facing them.

The revamped level design is one of the best aspects of the game. Most areas are much more open now — with a surplus of broader sections to explore and secrets to unravel. This novel approach regarding the levels is excellent and also refreshing to the series. Though, what caught my attention the most, was the much more extensive exploration system. Fortunately, that mechanic is excellent, and very much worthwhile. Similar to various horror titles, exploring each part of the map is essential for your survival. Here, investigating and exploring the various intriguing and breathtaking areas in search of crafting resources, ammunition, and all sorts of supplies can be the only thing that determines whether you die or stay alive to fight another day.

Resident Evil Village was, undoubtedly, my most delightful surprise this year thus far. I surely had a great time and have solely good things to say about the game — it absolutely has surpassed any expectations I had. It was a great experience from start to finish. I really liked how every area felt different, so it never got repetitive. [h1] Resident Evil Village: A Chaotic Blend of Horror and CInema [/h1]

Resident Evil Village is a mixed bag of horror elements that caters to a wide range of tastes, but this concoction, while intriguing initially, becomes overwhelming and unbalanced as you delve deeper. Just like sipping a complex smoothie, the first few sips are delightful, dark, and brooding, but as you continue, it turns fiery and wild, leaving you with a confusing aftertaste.

In this game, you once again step into the shoes of Ethan Winters, the same resilient yet bewildered protagonist from Resident Evil 7. This time, he's found himself in a chilling, snow-covered village teeming with lycanthropes instead of kids playing. The game manages to blend action and fear effectively during its first half. It starts with a hair-raising introduction that leads you through a village that's as monstrous as its furry inhabitants. Silence dominates the atmosphere, and every creak or snap of a twig sends shivers down your spine. Resources are scarce, firepower is limited, and fights are genuinely perilous. It's an unsettling crime scene that defies understanding, but you know you'll return to uncover the truth. Resident Evil Village shines when it embraces this patient, eerie atmosphere.

One of the early locations you explore is Dimitrescu's Castle, a grand fortress inhabited by a formidable lady, her diabolical daughters, and classic Resident Evil puzzles. More importantly, the castle preserves the village's eerie ambiance. The pacing is superb as you navigate its enigmatic puzzles and hidden passages, all while trying to ignore the suffocating silence.

But not everything in this game is flawless. Some moments prioritize action over fear, with boss fights feeling choreographed rather than genuine tests of survival. This pattern continues through most of the game, where significant encounters feel more like rehearsals with strict cues to follow. However, one location stands out as an exception.

As you progress, Resident Evil Village takes a turn. The village transforms into a hub world with four different zones, each home to one of the game's villains. The area you visit right after escaping the castle is especially exceptional, but I can't reveal any details about it without spoilers. Suffice it to say, it's a nightmarish and inventive experience that will keep you on your toes. It's a moment of vulnerability in the game, and it's masterful in how it plays with your fears.

Each return to the hub world keeps things fresh. The village subtly evolves to reflect your absence, with weather changes and subtle alterations that make revisiting areas feel rewarding. You may find new tools, like keys, during your adventures, making it satisfying to unlock previously inaccessible spots. These moments of discovery, such as finding new weapons or mysterious treasures, add depth to the gameplay.

Resident Evil Village is visually stunning, with detailed environments and intricate objects that bring its world to life. While the game ran smoothly on my RTX 2070-equipped system, I experienced one crash during a cutscene. This occurred during an early review build, so it may not reflect the final product.

The change in tone during the latter half of the game is kind of jarring. Action increasingly supersedes the horror aspect, and the abundance of weapons feels out of place. The introduction of the Duke, a shopkeeper who offers supplies and gun upgrades, makes resource scarcity less meaningful. By the end, the game prioritizes shooting over suspense and unpredictability.

As Resident Evil Village nears its conclusion, it spirals into chaos, with sequences that feel more suited to Call of Duty than a survival horror game. The transition from a chilling, unknown world to action-packed shootouts is unsettling, and the fear of running out of ammo replaces the fear of the unknown. The game sacrifices its unpredictable, chilling atmosphere for more straightforward gunfights.

Despite this shift, the game's story remains engaging. Ethan Winters' predicament hooks you from the beginning, and the conclusion, while messy, ties up loose ends and leaves room for more questions, a challenging feat for a long-running series.

In the end, Resident Evil Village tries to cater to a broad audience, but this ambition comes at the cost of balance. The early horror-focused sections are exceptional, but the game loses its way as it approaches the end, favoring action over fear. Despite this, it remains compelling.

Overall it's a wonderful game and it's a nice change of pace. The serialization and cinimatic focus of recent Resident Evil titles is something I'm enjoying and I'm hoping to see where Ethan's daughter plays in the next game.

Serious question: who is this game for? RE8 is a strange, incestuous mix of Resident Evil 4 and 7, but it isn't as good as either save for graphics. Being a sequel to 7, it takes place after that game and uses its first-person gameplay, but with several thoughtlessly-repeated mechanics and concepts from 4 without any understanding of why they were implemented in the first place.
 
The inventory system is the big one. RE8 initially presents itself as more of a survival horror title, but it has no real inventory management. Space is never an issue, so you can pretty much carry whatever you want at all times. Having space at all is basically rendered pointless because crafting materials for healing fluid, ammo, and explosives don't take up any space. The created items do take up space, but you can mitigate that by only crafting them when you need them since you can carry unlimited crafting materials. I only ran out of space ONE (1) time and that was solved by rotating one item. In RE4, weapon attachments took up space and continued to do so even if you had them equipped, so you had to sacrifice space if you wanted to use them. The attachments in RE8 only take up space so long as they are unattached from their corresponding guns. Once you equip them, they're removed from your inventory and can't be removed from the gun or sold; the decision makes itself. Furthermore, you're never strapped for ammo since you can just buy it from the merchant. In fact, I was literally given free ammo and a healing item as pre-order bonus. The purchasable resources and practically non-existent inventory management really take away from any tension during gameplay. There's literally no point in having inventory space like this if you aren't going to be limited by it. 

On the topic of combat and weapons, every new handgun or shotgun you get is a flat-out upgrade over the previous ones. They don't have different abilities or characteristics that would give any reason to utilize them like in RE4 (piercing, spread, speed, crit chance). People still argue about which is the superior handgun between the blacktail or the red-9 and make legitimate arguments for both. The same cannot be said about RE8's weapons. RE7's combat was mediocre at best, but it was perfectly serviceable for survival horror. I think even the staunchest defenders of RE7 will agree that its last third is the weakest due to increased linearity and focus on combat. Instead of fixing that, RE8 literally doubles down on the worst parts of 7 for its latter half. The combat is just not a good fit for RE4-style shooting galleries. You aren't spending the majority of time in one interconnected area and resources are abundant, so you never really need to make a choice about whether to engage in combat or not and clear out a specific area. The best option is almost always to kill every enemy in a given area. In RE8, there are no specialized melee moves, the guns aren’t satisfying to use, and there are few (if any) context-sensitive enemy reactions (shooting enemy legs to make them kneel, making enemies drop dynamite or torches, shooting enemies by ledges to make them fall). I occasionally made some Lycans fall off ledges, but the opportunity rarely ever arises. You can set enemies on fire, but I only remember doing this once to solve a puzzle (admittedly a pretty clever one). The point is: these systems are in the game, but aren't utilized nearly enough. Ultimately, RE8 can't cement itself as either solid action or survival horror. 
 
In terms of areas, the village, castle, and doll house are all great. The other areas, while graphically-impressive, are quite bland. The game makes a good first impression in the first half. The initial village assault is frantic and intense, as you have to fend off several Lycans similar to the opening survival bit in RE4. I feel that a lot of people will find blasting Lycans off of a rooftop and barricading doorways to be a highlight of the game. The castle is what I expected and wanted the entire game to be: puzzle-like progression in a semi-open map with stalker enemies. Dimitrescu and her daughters aren't that difficult to avoid, but things can get pretty nerve-wracking when they start appearing unscripted, especially when two of them show up at the same time. Puzzles here aren’t challenging, but it's acceptable given that the area is early and at least attempted classic RE level design. The dollhouse is a change of pace, but it is expertly done. The emptiness and initial lack of any music is really eerie. I was super tense during the segment and was intentionally walking slowly. You have your weapons taken away for a majority of the segment and solve some more admittedly-basic puzzles, but the incredible atmosphere and sound design of that area make up for it. Although, I can see why some may find it tedious, especially on repeat playthroughs. 
 
The reservoir, though, is extremely dull and uninteresting. Kind of hilarious how the giant fish can only get you on specific boards, which basically kills all tension. I won't compare it to the giant fish from RE4 because that isn't gonna end well for RE8. This area also lacks any original enemies, which is highly disappointing because aquatic enemies could've been really freaky (like some zombified anglerfish or mermaids). Stronghold is just a forgettable, linear action sequence without anything going for it. Factory is the only other major area after the castle. It looks decent and some of the enemies are cool, but it’s so far removed from the tone and aesthetics of everything prior that it literally feels like a different game at that point, and not in a good way.
 
RE8 has a mercenaries mode, but it's easily the worst iteration of it. There are no extra characters or loadouts; you buy/sell what you want between fights. You have to move around to different part of the map and can only kill a set number of enemies on a generous timer instead of an endless horde. The best strategy is always to buy a single weapon and upgrade it as much as you can. It's braindead and offers no flexibility. In previous games, you rarely had to actually look for enemies to kill. They would always come to you. Most enemies in RE8's mercs are those Dark Souls-wannabe zombies(?) that aren't fast or aggressive, so you have to actively go and look for them. It's not so bad in early levels, but this makes the factory an absolute trash fire. It's incredibly easy to miss a single enemy that you didn’t see behind some random corner and lose your combo looking for the twat. In previous games, if a story level didn’t work in mercs, they would just make a new level built for the mode using the same assets, but we don’t get that here. Part of the appeal of mercenaries was getting to play as characters unavailable in the story like villains. RE8’s first-person perspective may not make the idea seem novel, but it would’ve been a better way to handle special abilities rather than giving randomly-selected, boring upgrades. Chris could have an expanded melee system or one of Dimitrescu's daughters could do quick dodges or special attacks by turning into a swarm of insects. Hell, I would've settled for even less. If they just swapped the player hands and voice lines, that would've made me spend a little more time on it. I'm spit balling ideas here, but it's pretty clear that RE8's mercs mode is bare-bones and half-assed. It also accentuates how weak the combat is. #notmymercenaries
 
Again, who is this game for? There's no real inventory management, resources are never scarce, the few puzzles are basic, and the game stops trying to be scary in any capacity halfway through, so it's clearly not for survival horror fans. The gameplay is a straight downgrade from RE4 in every regard, so it isn't good action either. It isn't even a bad game, but it’s not worth full price. resident evil village might be capcom’s greatest feat yet for the franchise. 

resident evil 7 took players by surprise, steering the series in a markedly different direction. up until seven, the resident evil games were primarily action-oriented survival horror experiences. this approach wasn't inherently flawed, as it aligned with capcom's vision for the franchise. however, when seven was released, it astonished players by deeply embracing horror elements, setting a high bar for it’s sequel.

this is where it gets tricky. while seven was largely successful, some fans found it “too scary” or considered it a deviation from the franchise’s roots. village had to balance appeasing fans of seven and long-time enthusiasts who preferred the classic survival horror with an action-centric style.

so, what became of village? it largely adhered to the classic style. the house beneviento section, where the game truly leaned into horror, was particularly notable. stripped of all tools, players found themselves helpless in a dark, eerie setting, a homage to seven that resulted in a gripping experience. besides this, moments of genuine fear occurred when facing lycans, thanks to their element of surprise. the village environment allowed lycans to camouflage perfectly, often necessitating a second look to spot them. the game skillfully used music to build tension and surprise especially during the blood-soaked basement section. while the game leaned more towards action than pure horror, this wasn’t necessarily a drawback. in the end, resident evil village turned out to be phenomenal.

even though this game was released for last-generation consoles, it stands as one of the best-looking games capcom has ever produced. from the intricately crafted romanian architecture of castle dimitrescu to the old-school layout of house beneviento, every environment is meticulously crafted, offering a visual feast. heisenberg’s factory, with its modern look, still manages to awe with its detailed design.

as for gameplay, ethan moves particularly the same as before, but there's a wider array of firearms available this time. this includes classic handguns, rocket launchers, a laser sword, and more, marking a step up from seven. ammo scarcity remains a concern, maintaining the survival aspect. the firearms complement this game well, much like the firearms of seven did to themselves. the lycan are particularly unique and agile, providing a fresh challenge compared to the zombies of previous games.

the game also rewards players for exploration. village is filled with open areas that are fairly linear yet interconnected. hidden treasures and a optional boss fight await those who venture off the beaten path. revisiting areas with new keys and items often reveals previously inaccessible treasures and weapons, enhancing the sense of discovery.

let’s talk about karl heisenberg as a character. everything about him was phenomenal, the character design complimented with neil newbon’s voice acting. his motivations throughout the game and his factory, everything about him was just memorable.

additionally , there’s a mercenaries mode. all resident evil games could benefit from this mode, which offers an arcade-like experience centered around fun. players can control characters like alcina, heisenberg, chris, and ethan, each offering unique abilities. I wasn’t particularly impressed with chris redfield and the BSAA’s involvement throughout the game. they accompanied ethan but mostly stayed idle, only contributing at the last minute. their aid in the fight against heisenberg was noteworthy, but chris’s sporadic appearances felt underwhelming. surprising, yes but underwhelming.

capcom concludes the ethan winters saga with a splendid narrative. ethan’s character  and the overall storytelling are exceptional, despite some corny dialogue. most resident evil games pit protagonists with supernatural foes against seemingly ordinary humans. whilst offering fun gameplay, these characters seem flawed in design; chris is the boulder-punching a-hole, leon was practically superhuman in four, and ethan has insane regenerative abilities. however, village explains ethan’s abilities as the game nears its end. additionally, providing a satisfying conclusion to his story.

village has borrowed elements from its predecessor, such as the duke’s emporium, among other things. however, I feel these are basic components of a well-established franchise that more games could benefit from. just as resident evil 7 served as a sketch for resident evil 2 to some extent, resident evil village does the same for resident evil 4. nevertheless, both games have managed to stand out uniquely on their own.

thank you, ethan winters. 
you will be missed.

With that being said, this review is going to be one big hot take because I am a little conflicted about my feelings after playing it… I can’t decide if this one dethrones [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] as my favorite RE or not!

This is not a decision I take lightly. [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] is one of my favorite games ever made. It’s one of very few games that I’ve played over and over again throughout the years. It's recognized as a classic that innovated games for years after it came out. Hell, over-the-shoulder cameras are still the standard for third-person games and QTEs are still used today – for better or worse. [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] does not do anything that innovative.

But [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] is so fucking cool. From start to finish, every environment is engaging. Each of the villains is interesting and entertaining (even Moreau, in my opinion). The story is, of course, nonsense – but it's compelling nonsense that had me wondering what was going to happen next. These are all things that I’d be hard pressed to say about [i]Resident Evil 4[/i]. (Remember Krauser and how the only memorable thing about him is the crappy QTE boss battle? Remember the yawn inducing island area? I’d rather forget those things, honestly.)

The humor is back from RE4, and I couldn't be happier about it. Horror comedy is my favorite genre of… well, any medium. This game is absolutely ridiculous and still manages to be spooky. I think Sturm encapsulates this well: he made me laugh as I pissed my pants and that's just the best feeling in the world. 

The action feels fluid, though, admittedly, I missed Leon’s roundhouse kick to stagger big groups of baddies. One of the achievements alludes to pushing an enemy after blocking – maybe it functions the same way? I'm not sure; I didn't know about it before beating the game.

Then there's the hot button issue: this game is not long. It's not massive. Maybe some DLC will make it girthy in the future. However, it doesn't overstay its welcome, either, and I'm glad that this one avoided that issue, unlike others in the series. It's part of why I felt this one is consistently good; Capcom trimmed all the fat and put put out an excellent product.

Okay. Okay, after putting everything down in writing, I think I'm ready to say it: 

[i]Resident Evil Village[/i] has supplanted [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] as my favorite game in the series and, consequently, as one of my favorite games of all time. 

Of course, this doesn't mean I'm tossing RE4 in the trash. For all the negative things I mentioned in this review, it's still a phenomenal game that holds up very well today. Honestly, I think the point of this review is to urge you to try this one if you’re a fan of RE4 and reluctant to give it a go. If you haven’t, do it. As I mentioned before, there’s a really good chance that you’ll enjoy this one, too.

TL;DR: 
While visually stunning, RE8 delivers a weak story and misses the mark on most classic RE features like puzzles, inventory management and player path choice. Although this is a negative review, I’d recommend RE8 even to non RE fans with the caveat to only buy it on sale 50% off or more at this point. Read on if you want to specifically know why.

This review will be spoiler free, so you are welcome to read at any point of any subheading. Queue the save room music and the typewriter clacking sounds.

Basis of My Perspective: 
The Resident Evil franchise is something that I enjoy a lot. Personally, I have played nearly every RE game: RE 0-8, Revelations 1&2, Code Veronica, Outbreak, Resistance and the RE-makes 1-3. During my time with these games, I’ve gotten to see what makes for great versions of RE and what doesn’t. Now, this is also somewhat subjective mind you, but I think I have a good handle on what players want out of a RE game. Feel free to disagree with any of what I write in the comments below. If you keep it constructive & civil I may respond to you, but I don’t feed trolls. For the record, I played RE8 on the standard difficulty with a completion time of ~11-12 hours and about 5 hours of Mercenaries content. 

Critique of Pacing:
This game is super linear and it is one of my biggest gripes. It almost feels like it is on rails a good 80% of  the game. There is only ever one path, except for a couple of spots where you can monkey around for extra loot. Every other door you pass will be locked and only opened in one sequence. There is a lack of suspense due to this linearity. In most other RE games, a player is allowed to have a few options simultaneously available to them at all points of the game, except during the ending sequence. This is usually coupled with puzzles that a player is expected to deduce clues to and solve along their exploration. While RE8 allows you to double back, usually it is an irrelevant waste of time.

Critique of Puzzles:
Writing this part will be simple, much like the puzzles in RE8. One of the main appeals in the RE series for me is having to use problem solving skills at the strategic scale in combination with shooting skills at the tactical/situational level. This dual requirement of both skill sets is a key component of what makes a good RE game. In great RE games, I felt like I was using brains and brawn to take down some evil plot. It was like me and my character were out witting and out gunning some cabal of nefarious jerks. In RE8 the puzzles are so laughable that I only had trouble with 1 and that was because I was too distracted IRL to notice when I walked by the object in game. The protagonist in RE8 is no sleuth, the bad guys are just that dumb in this one. Disappointing.

Critique of Story (Still Spoiler Free):
The story for RE8 is only there for ticking boxes. The motivations for the antagonists in this game are never explained well and the explanations that are provided are very weak. Events just seem to happen and the protagonists respond reactively. The plot is very flimsy despite a decent chunk of cutscenes. I don’t think I can write more without spoiling something, so I’ll leave it here.

Critique of Inventory Management:
You almost always have enough space for everything. There is no struggle to pick and choose which guns to bring, you can have em’ all. This makes for a boring experience. Again, going back to deducing as you explore in the other RE games, typically your character isn’t allowed to carry everything. So, this means that you should be paying attention to what is likely up ahead and plan accordingly. Did you just come across a lab note and photo about some experimental bioweapon in the next room? Yeah, normally in a RE game, you’d have taken note of some weakness to acid or flame rounds, or possibly some freezing weakness in fight preparation. In RE8 you get these notes… after you just figured it out on your own by killing a version of whatever is lying dead in the previous room.

Another misstep is the crafting of items. In a world that strives for photorealism, everything appears as potentially scrap metal, or rusted scrap metal. Making it a component of some bullet formula is immersion breaking. On the fly ammo making with garbage from the environment that doesn’t take up inventory space is silly. Why even have a backpack with a grid layout when you make it meaningless? 

Critique of Visuals:
This is where RE8 shines. Like most new games, the tradeoff of better visuals for less substantiative gameplay has been made. The shading, textures, and especially the reflections of metallic/wet surfaces are spot on. It is truly a gorgeous game. For those interested, I ran the game 1920x1080 on a RTX 3060 on relatively high settings. 

Overall Critique:
Personally, I think that RE8 is a slightly above average game for its contemporaries, but only an OK RE game. I do not think it deserves accolades of any kind. It is my estimation that the bar is so incredibly low for games right now, that since this one came out fully completed and is not a total trainwreck, it stands out against the dismal array of other current offerings.

What RE8 tried to do was emulate RE4, but failed. The plot is too thin to not want to poke holes in it as you are playing. It relies on visual aesthetics to induce immersion, but when every other choice seems to somewhat break that immersion, it falls flat. As I sit here writing this review, I am contemplating whether or not to play RE8 ever again, or simply remove it from my hard drive. Honestly, my gut says it is too unappealing to try to play the game again. This is coming from someone who beat RE4 at least 3 times and played countless hours of mercenaries. 

Where RE4 shined RE8 misses. RE4 was more linear than RE8, but it had such better story lines, ammo management considerations, puzzles and special melee moves, that you kind of accepted the linearity as a method to keep the excitement up and not get bogged down in the searching/sleuthing. RE8 takes this linear approach, but then makes the main playable protagonist feel like a couch potato compared to Leon. RE4 also, adds this beautifully crafted, multilayered plot that is intriguing, albeit a bit campy. You knew why Leon was there, but what was Wesker and Umbrella up to? Was Ada a friend or foe? WTF is wrong with Salazar? There were questions you wanted answers to and were willing to shoot endless quantities of mobs in the head for. RE8 does not have this.

Another example of the failure to understand why RE4 works is the Mercenaries game mode. RE4’s Mercenaries mode was a fast paced, white knuckle, explosion filled, roundhouse kick to the face of excitement. RE8’s Mercenaries mode has you waiting for floppy death animations to stop so that you can pick up all of the dumb coin drops that are the basis of the scoring/progression. Frustrating. Not to mention having to revisit the shop after every match. Just gimme the damn guns and let me pew pew some heads until they explode.

There are countless more choices that are off about RE8 that make you wonder #1 where is this franchise going? #2 Do the developers understand their own past successes? #3 Do I even ever bother buying a RE game at full sticker ever again? As to the 3rd question, I’d say no. Not until something amazing comes out from the franchise. I played RE8 for ~20 hours of gameplay and got what seems like zero grand scheme plot development and mediocre entertainment. There are games in my catalog that are cheaper, but yet have enthralled me exponentially more than RE8 did. I can take the low play hours of an RE game if those play hours are fantastic. I’d consider it like breaking out the top shelf liquor, an indulgence that I’d be willing to splurge on, for the right spirit. Sadly, RE8 isn’t it. Capcom needs to look at RE-1&2 Remakes as the future formula of this franchise, or if they want to do a campy, rompy RE4 clone, then do it right.

Impeccable atmosphere. The snowy village, the opulent castle, the feeling of a place stuck in time where something isn't quite right. There's an unsettling stillness to everything that lingers even when you get attacked by the monsters, a constant feeling of being watched by whatever might be lurking in the shadows. 

It can be peaceful at times, but the tension is always there. You know it's not safe, but you can't help but be mesmerized by the overwhelming beauty of the landscape. 

Inside the village itself, you might feel somewhat too big, out of place, but as soon as you look around and truly take in the size of the mountains and everything surrounding you on a larger scale, an inescapable feeling of loneliness and hopelessness takes over. And yet, Ethan keeps pushing on. His resilience is so raw, so human. So powerful.

Would have loved an option to team up with Heisenberg. His defiant demeanor is extremely appealing, and I feel that with enough tactfulness involved, he could have been convinced to elaborate a new plan to take down Miranda together with Ethan, without weaponizing Rose. Despite his roughness, his anger and resentment towards Miranda, he's incredibly smart and shows a level consideration towards others and life itself that you don't see in the other lords, especially regarding his own experiments. His focus on using Rose's powers in order to defeat Miranda seems to come from a place of self-doubt and insecurity. Despite being the most powerful of the four Lords, he still doesn't believe he's strong enough to take Miranda down for good, even with Ethan's help. His diary entries are particularly heartbreaking; Heisenberg just wants to be free, to be in charge of himself, and after decades of being mistreated, abused and experimented on, he knows he will only be able to rest if he takes down the person who inflicted all that pain on him with his own hands.

I truly hope someday we get a DLC/spin-off focused on the four Lords. There are endless possibilities for such interesting characters, especially in the Resident Evil world, and it would be a shame to see all that potential wasted.

[i][b]I just wanted to share that even if you’re not familiar with Resident Evil 7, you can absolutely enjoy Village without feeling lost. The game is so thoughtful and kind in offering a little recap of the previous story right at the beginning, so anyone new to the series can easily get up to speed. However, if you’re looking for a deeper emotional connection and a richer understanding of the storyline, playing Biohazard from 2017 might make the experience even more special.[/b]

At first, the plot might seem straightforward, but it’s so much more than it appears. At its heart, it’s a touching tale of a father on a desperate journey to find his daughter, full of twists and mysteries that uncover the roots of the dreaded Umbrella Corporation. As the story unfolds, it becomes even more captivating, with an ending that will leave you absolutely stunned. Although the game isn’t overly long—about ten hours—you’ll find yourself wanting to return to uncover hidden treasures and side missions that add a little more magic to the experience. And with the return of the Mercenaries mode, there's always something fun to challenge you.

As for the characters, there’s something so intriguing about figures like Lady Dimitrescu and Salvatore Moreau. But what really seemed to take the breath away of those who tested the game were the breathtaking, realistic environments. From the chilling atmosphere in Dimitrescu Castle to the unsettling beauty of Heisenberg’s factory, every corner of the game is filled with so much detail and care. Even the eerie moments are crafted so beautifully—it's as if the game finds a way to make the scary feel strangely beautiful. One exception might be the encounter with the second boss, Donna Beneviento, but even in these dark moments, the setting’s richness really stands out.

As with every game in this series, Resident Evil Village gently encourages you to be curious and explore every nook and cranny. You’ll need to pay close attention to the items you find, as some of them require a little assembly or disassembly to be truly useful. One lovely thing about this chapter is that many of the items you find have longer-lasting uses, which makes everything feel so meaningful. Plus, there are areas that you’ll want to revisit later, which adds to the charm, almost like building with Lego blocks.

The map in Resident Evil Village is incredibly intuitive, making it easier to navigate and discover areas you’ve yet to explore. But I have to admit, for those who love collecting everything, it can be a little tricky to stay on top of all the hidden treasures.

Even though the ending might feel a bit drawn out, every minute of time spent is so worth it. The story is rich, emotional, and complex, with stunning visuals and villains who are beautifully developed. Resident Evil Village brings Ethan Winters' journey to a close in a way that’s truly satisfying, with gameplay that’s both terrifying and exhilarating. Above all, it’s a powerful story about family, hope, love, and the strength to never give up.[/i]

After finishing RE9, I went back and completed Resident Evil Village — and honestly, this game is great.

I’m not a huge Resident Evil veteran, but Village really pulled me in. Great atmosphere, memorable locations and bosses, satisfying combat, and a really nice balance between horror and action. It constantly keeps things interesting, and the whole game feels polished and fun.

It’s not perfect though. There are definitely some frustrating moments, especially on Hardcore, where the game can feel more exhausting than challenging. The Shadows of Rose DLC was good too, but on higher difficulty it had a few pretty annoying sections.

Still, overall, Resident Evil Village is a fantastic experience.
Lady D stole the spotlight, Heisenberg was fun as hell, and Ethan survives everything through pure pain tolerance.

10 torn-off-and-glued-back Ethan hands out of 10.

RE7 was already a great game, and this one is even better. It improves on a lot of things from the previous game.

The pacing is really good. Each area feels different, with its own vibe, so it never gets boring. Some parts are pure horror, others are more action packed or puzzle heavy.

The characters are super memorable, especially Lady D and Heisenberg. The ending is really good and explains a lot. Ethan’s story wraps up in a satisfying way too.

Performance wise, it runs great, and the environments are just beautiful. The castle especially looks amazing.

Buy this game, it’s worth it.

It was such a well done round off to Ethan's story, to me this game is still very Resident Evil at its core, it had great different horror elements throughout and amazing enemy designs. RE8 shines with fantastic character development and graphical detail. The worlds are beautifully rendered, making you want to explore them, but you'll also be done with the game in just 7-10 hours.

The Mercenary Mode offers a bit of variety, but in my opinion, it doesn't measure up to any of the other Resident Evil games. It simply feels like a poor imitation of Killing Floor; I found the Mercenary Mode in the RE4 remake to be much better.

The enemies are very diverse and offer plenty of variety. I especially loved the horror elements; the potential was well utilized. These disturbing scenes created a completely new experience. The story is also well told, and the cutscenes are very well done.

Resident Evil Biohazard and Resident Evil Village are the best games in the series. I've already written a review of RE Biohazard, so let's talk about RE Village.

This game best depicts the “horror” genre; it is not oversaturated with jump scares, scary music, or darkness.  Each character is unique, with their own story, and frightening in different ways.  I would like to be like Miss Dimitrescu, walking around my huge luxurious castle in a long dress, wearing red lipstick and hunting men.  Well, okay, let's skip this point.

The uniqueness of the game is that in addition to horror elements, it contains a plot with deep meaning.  I haven't seen horror like this often.  Basically, you go around killing creatures just to kill creatures.  The plot does not touch the soul, but here at the end I shed a tear. 

Of course, the game also has its downsides.  For example, not all glass breaks, bullet marks don't always remain, but the game is so beautiful that I can close my eyes to it.

To conclude, Ethan Winters is the best father.

It is a step up in term of boss battles and enemy variety and combat, but has less horror than RE7 overall. Except that one segment which is terrifying, beyond that other levels has quite a bit of combat. 

Story-wise it connects to previous RE games and leading toward RE 9 and has an excellent ending.

Other complains i have is The Mercenaries in RE Village. It's not the same as Mercenaries in RE4, RE5, RE6 as they are about surviving and making score until the time runs out. But in RE Village it's about knowing where the enemies will spawn and killing and keeping combo and run to the next area until the last enemy is killed. The reward for beating all mercenaries stages with SS rank is very weak and unsatisfying for the effort you need to put in to get it.

It's a pretty good game so i highly recommend it to anyone who is new to the series.

Note: the DLCs are for gun cosmetics, RE7 in-game screen effects and starting supplies. So you should only get it for cosmetics reason or supplies, the RE7 handgun isn't worth it. You can't upgrade it and it will be obsolete very soon into the game.

I've gone through six playthroughs of this game and can't get enough of it. It captures the gothic aesthetic perfectly and its eerie atmosphere. Every character progresses throughout the plot so beautifully with their motives and struggles. And Ethan is easily one of the best written characters in the RE universe. Capcom did take a wildly different approach with this one (especially after the events of Biohazard), but it was balanced into the main plotline very well. I especially love how they did Chris' character for this game, but my only complaint is his attitude towards Ethan up until the Heisenberg fight and the reason for it made no sense to me. But I guess it could be cause he suffers from PTSD and massive anxiety, Boulder buddy needs a margarita and a holiday on a resort, away from all this bioterrorism.

However if you haven't played 7 you might be a little confused of some of the things that happen, there is a recap worth watching if you need a reminder of the events prior to 8. 

The game is really tense on hardcore and is one of the harder RE games, especially cause I have been playing with a controller on my big tv rather than K&M. However if 80 FOV bothers you in games, you might want to pass as it isn't changeable. 

This game is heavily inspired by RE4, built with that game and the past 3 titles. This game takes a lot of the elements those games did right. However the beginning of the game doesn't guide you very well, so you're going to be scrabbling trying to understand what the hell is happening. That took away from the horror as I was too confused to be scared. Playing on hardcore doesn't help, after dying all the tension built up goes away, and confusion is all that is left. 

After the awkward start, that is basically the village part of RE4 redone, the game was a lot more enjoyable. It's not an easy game, and after 4 hours I've only beaten one of the 5 main bosses and it was good enough to write my review now. If you were on the fence maybe that'll make the purchase easier.
